source.title: Trustworthy Efficient Communication for Distributed Learning Using LQ-SGD Algorithm
source.authors: Hong-Yang Li; Li Bai; Caesar Wu; Mohammed Chadli; S. Mammar; P. Bouvry

page_placements.theme: Distributed updates and communication affect accuracy and efficiency

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper; no cut-off or garbling that prevents extraction was apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports test accuracy for distributed gradient-compression methods, but does not measure train error, the train–test gap, or a behavior named by any claim version.
record.gate_note: Test-accuracy comparisons are relevant to held-out performance but cannot establish whether training and test error diverge. The paper does not test random-label memorization, width, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, adaptive optimizers, batch size, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example removal.
record.test_reason: The experiments vary gradient compression and compression rank, measuring accuracy, communication, computation and reconstruction SSIM. None tests V1–V8. Compression rank is neither network width nor batch size, and these SGD variants are not adaptive optimizers of the kind named in V4. Missing training error is not the decisive exclusion: several versions can be tested with held-out accuracy when the relevant experimental comparison is present.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors present LQ-SGD as reducing communication while retaining competitive accuracy and convergence, and report lower gradient-inversion reconstruction SSIM for compression methods than Original SGD. They acknowledge that evaluation is limited to image classification and does not cover very large architectures.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares distributed gradient-compression methods and reports validation accuracy; it does not use the random-label, width, architecture, optimizer, batch-size, regularization, sharpness, or example-removal procedures in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and compression method/rank vary; the text reports test accuracy by method on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNIST.

fits_no_version.finding: Compression methods produce different held-out accuracies: LQ-SGD versus Original SGD is 0.9290 versus 0.9432 on CIFAR-10, 0.7181 versus 0.7445 on CIFAR-100, and 0.9939 versus 0.9940 on MNIST.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient compression can change image-classification accuracy, with effects depending on the compression method and dataset.

record.problems: The accuracy tables report no uncertainty estimates and no corresponding training errors, so the train–test gap cannot be assessed. The supplied text describes ImageNet results in Figure 4 but does not give exact accuracy values there.
record.rows_left_out: ImageNet accuracy comparisons across LQ-SGD ranks and Original SGD are described in the text and shown in Figure 4, but exact values are not stated; those comparisons are omitted because the paper supplies no tabulated values and the claim's train–test gap is not measured. SSIM results in Figure 5 concern gradient-inversion reconstruction, not the generalization claim.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and the paired natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
Network widening beyond zero training error and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures, local connectivity and initialization effects.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning breadth, decoupled weight decay and optimizer switching.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce large-batch penalties.
Dropout effects, small-data regimes, underfitting and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, generalization gaps and comparison with other generalization measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The record incorrectly says the text supplies no exact ImageNet accuracy: Section V-B states that rank-7 LQ-SGD matches Original SGD at 75% Top-1 accuracy after 300 epochs. This is outside V1–V8 and does not require a missing claim-evidence row. Citations to Goyal and Shallue concern communication and scaling context; they do not establish a batch-size test here.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and the effects of tuning, weight decay, or switching optimizers.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the train–test gap.
Effects of removing memorized training examples.

relation.reason: The paper discusses preserving held-out accuracy during gradient compression without testing or relying on any named claim version.

tranche.reason: The experiments compare gradient-compression methods and compression ranks; none tests or uses V1–V8. Compression rank is neither network width nor batch size, and the methods do not test adaptive optimizers against SGD.

source_check.notes: All twelve rows accurately report benchmark results but provide no claim evidence; R4, R8 and R12 are the study's own method comparisons. Contrary to the pack's coverage note, Section V.B explicitly reports 75% ImageNet Top-1 accuracy after 300 epochs at rank 7.
